title: The Sun Through Its Gates
sum: The Astronomical Book opens with its title: the book of how the lights of the sky move, as the angel Uriel showed them to Enoch. The first law is the sun's. Six gates in the east and six in the west mark where it rises and sets. The sun spends thirty days in each gate, moving north toward midsummer and back south toward midwinter, and the day grows and shrinks in eighteenths: from 9 and 9 at the equinox to 12 and 6 at midsummer.

Every third month has a thirty-first day "because of its sign," and the chapter adds it all up: "The year comes to exactly 364 days" (72:32). That number, 52 weeks with nothing left over, is the heart of this book, and the source of a long quarrel among Jews over the right calendar.
readings: As a description of the sky, the chapter is a schematic model: real sunrise points do move along the horizon, but the 16-hour longest day fits a latitude far north of Jerusalem, and the true year is about 365¼ days. It belongs with Babylonian schemes such as MUL.APIN, and it is the oldest Jewish work of astronomy we have.

The chapter's point is that the sky obeys a law that God commanded (72:36). The sun "does not grow smaller and does not rest" (72:37). Order in the heavens is a picture of the faithfulness the righteous should show, and a rebuke to those who keep the wrong days (82:4–5).

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox churches read this chapter as part of Henok's revealed book, showing that God set the sun's course. Their own church year follows the Alexandrian 365-day calendar, and Ethiopian scholars of the reckoning of time (baḥrä ḥassab) have long studied these chapters.
views.H: Most scholars see the oldest Jewish astronomy here, drawn from Babylonian learning in the Persian or early Hellenistic period and written in Aramaic by the 200s BC. The Ethiopic is a shortened form of a much longer Aramaic book.
views.N: The chapter is background for New Testament talk of "days, months, seasons and years" (Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16) and for debates about the date of the Last Supper (see chapter 82).
views.J: At Qumran this calendar shaped the community's life; the rabbis kept the moon-based year and set Enoch aside. Medieval Jewish writers rarely knew the book.
views.W: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers value the chapter as a window into how Jews before Christ read Genesis 1:14, not as a true account of the sky.

The four 31-day months (3, 6, 9, 12) hold the four added days of 75:1–2 and 82:4–6. Each quarter has 30 + 30 + 31 = 91 days, which is exactly 13 weeks.

The 2 to 1 ratio of longest day to shortest, the gates on the horizon and the 360-day ideal year with added days all have parallels in the Babylonian compendium MUL.APIN (Hunger and Pingree). The ratio fits latitude about 49°, not Judea (Neugebauer). The scheme came to Jewish scribes as learned tradition, and they gave it a new frame: not omens from the gods, but laws set by the one Creator.

In the Aramaic scrolls the Astronomical Book was far longer than the Ethiopic. 4Q208 and 4Q209 held a day-by-day table of the sun and moon that the Ge'ez summarizes in a few verses (see the note on 73:1).

echoes: Genesis 1:14–18; Psalm 19:4–6; Psalm 104:19; Ecclesiastes 1:5; Isaiah 30:26; Jeremiah 31:35; Jubilees 6:32

settings.what: Uriel's lessons on the lights, the winds and the world
settings.by: Enoch, reporting what the angel Uriel showed him
settings.to: Enoch's son Methuselah, who is to pass the teaching on (76:14; 79:1)
settings.when: in the story, before the flood, during Enoch's journeys with Uriel
settings.why: To show that the sun, moon and stars keep exact laws God set, and so to teach the true year of 364 days. Inside the story, Methuselah receives knowledge no one else has, to hand down to Noah and beyond.
settings.readers: A circle of learned Jewish scribes in Judea, probably with priestly ties, in the 200s BC or earlier. They knew Babylonian-style astronomy and cared that the temple's Sabbaths and feasts fell on the right days. The oldest Aramaic copies (4Q208–4Q211) come from the library later kept at Qumran.
views: Many scholars (Milik, VanderKam, Drawnel) think this is the oldest part of 1 Enoch, written in the 300s or 200s BC.
Others stress that its first readers were already arguing over the calendar with the temple authorities, as Jubilees and the Qumran texts later did.

traditions.q: Are angels in charge of the stars and the weather?
views: Yes. God governs creation through his angels, and 1 Enoch names Uriel as the angel over the lights. The church honors Uriel (Urael) as an archangel with his own feast days.

Thomas Aquinas taught that God governs bodily things through the angels (Summa Theologiae I, q. 110, a. 1), and the Catechism calls angels servants of God's plan in creation (Catechism 332). But the Church discourages naming angels other than Michael, Gabriel and Raphael (Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy, 2001, §217).

Angels serve God's providence over creation and the nations (Daniel 10:13; Deuteronomy 32:8, Greek). The church honors the archangels at the Synaxis of the Archangels (8 November), and common Orthodox use names seven, including Raphael and Uriel.

Angels are God's servants (Hebrews 1:14), but John Calvin warned against speculating about their ranks and offices (Institutes 1.14.4). God's providence rules nature directly, whatever servants he uses.

title: The Smaller Light
sum: After the sun comes the moon, "the smaller light" of Genesis 1:16. It rides a chariot driven by wind, and its light is "given to it by measure": at full, one seventh of the sun's. The chapter then follows the moon through the first days of its month, counting its light in sevenths and their halves, fourteenths.

The numbers in the Ge'ez are tangled, and Dillmann's text and the EOTC print disagree in places. Behind this short chapter stands a long Aramaic table, found at Qumran, that tracked the moon day by day beside the sun.

views.E: Read as part of Henok's revealed teaching: God gave the moon its law, and its changing light still serves the reckoning of the church's moveable feasts.
views.H: A summary of the Aramaic "synchronistic calendar" (4Q208–4Q209). Neugebauer showed that the fractions work as steps of one fourteenth a day.
views.J: The moon's role is the point of division. Sirach says the feasts are known from the moon (Sirach 43:6–8); the Enoch tradition, followed by Jubilees, ranks it below the sun.
views.W: Valued as evidence of ancient Jewish science and of a real dispute over the calendar, not as revelation about the moon.

deep.b: Picture the full moon cut into fourteen equal slices. In this scheme the moon gains one slice of light each day for fourteen days and loses one each day for fourteen more (73:5–8; 78:6–8). The first night it has only half a slice. Real moonlight does not grow in equal daily steps, but the scheme is easy to count, and it lines up neatly with the fourteen days from new moon to full.

title: Moon Months and Sun Years
sum: Uriel shows Enoch the moon's course through the months: how it swings through the gates in a few days, as the sun does in a year, and how it fills and empties of light. Enoch writes it all down (74:2).

Then come the sums. The sun and stars keep 364 days and "do not get ahead or fall behind by a single day" (74:12). The moon's year is shorter, and the chapter counts how far behind it falls in three, five and eight years. Three years is the useful number: the moon is then exactly one month behind.

views.E: Read as God's own ordering of the lights, revealed to Henok and written down by him. Ethiopian computus also works with cycles that bring sun and moon back into step.
views.H: The sums show a scribal school working out how to fit moon months into a 364-day year. The eight-year cycle may show contact with Greek reckoning.
views.N: Background for the calendar disputes behind Galatians 4:10 and Colossians 2:16, and for the priestly division of Abijah in Luke 1:5, which the Qumran texts also track.
views.J: Qumran's calendar scrolls use these very cycles. The rabbis kept the moon's months and added a thirteenth month when needed, by rules that, by Jewish tradition, were fixed in the 300s AD.
views.W: Of interest as the oldest Jewish attempt to reconcile sun and moon; the 364-day year itself drifts against the real seasons.

The three-year line is the key. After three years the moon is exactly one month behind, so adding a month every three years keeps the moon's months in step with the sun's year. The Qumran calendar scrolls (4Q319–4Q321) build six-year cycles on this idea and fit the turns of the twenty-four priestly divisions into them. The "six days" of 74:11 do not fit the table and seem to measure from a 360-day year.

Enoch "wrote down their positions" (74:2). In this book Enoch is above all a scribe, and the knowledge he writes is meant to be copied and studied. That is what its first readers did: the Aramaic copies at Qumran were working texts for people who counted days.

title: The Four Added Days
sum: The four extra days of the year, one at the end of each quarter, have their own angelic officers. They are "not counted" in the ordinary count of months, and "because of them people make mistakes" (75:2). Uriel, set by "the Lord of glory" over all the lights, shows Enoch the signs, seasons, years and days.

The chapter then turns back to the machinery of the sky: twelve gates in the sun's chariot that let out its rays and heat, windows that open in their season, and chariots that carry the stars that never set around the pole.

views.E: The angels' service on the four days shows that nothing in God's order is left unattended. The Ethiopian church honors Uriel as an archangel.
views.H: The polemic about the four days points to rival calendars of the time: a 360-day schematic year, or the moon. Jubilees 6 and the Qumran texts carry the same quarrel further.
views.N: The list "signs, seasons, years and days" comes from Genesis 1:14 and has an echo in Galatians 4:10.
views.J: For the Qumran community, getting these days wrong meant keeping God's feasts on the wrong days (Damascus Document 3:13–15).
views.W: Most churches read the angels over nature as poetry about God's care, and reject the claim that missing four days in the count is sin.

deep.b: If you count only twelve months of 30 days, your year is 360 days and every feast slides four days each year against the true 364-day count. Within a few years Passover would fall in the wrong week. For people who believed the 364-day year was God's own, that was not a small error: it meant celebrating God's holy days on ordinary days, and working on the true holy days. That is why Enoch, Jubilees and the Qumran texts speak of the calendar in the language of sin.

echoes: Genesis 1:14; Deuteronomy 4:19; Job 38:7; Job 38:31–33; Galatians 4:10; Jubilees 6:32–38

title: The Twelve Winds
sum: At the ends of the earth Enoch sees twelve more gates, three for each direction, and from them come the winds. Four bring "blessing and well-being": rain, dew, fruit and life. Eight bring punishment: heat, drought, cold, frost, locusts and ruin.

Enoch walks through them in order, east, south, north and west, and ends by speaking to his son: "I have shown you all their laws... my son Methuselah" (76:14). Aramaic fragments of this chapter survive at Qumran.

views.E: God rules the weather; blessing and punishment come from his storehouses at his command, as in the Psalms and Job.
views.H: A wind rose of twelve, like those of Greek writers, set inside a Near Eastern picture of the world. Its weather fits the land of Israel: hot east wind, rain from the west.
views.N: Compare the angels holding back the four winds in Revelation 7:1–3.
views.W: Read as an ancient description of weather that shares the Bible's conviction that wind and rain are in God's hands (Psalm 135:7; Jeremiah 10:13).

settings.when: after describing the twelve wind gates
settings.why: It reminds the reader that the whole lesson is a father's teaching to his son, to be kept in the family and passed on.
settings.readers: A circle of learned Jewish scribes in Judea, probably with priestly ties, in the 200s BC or earlier. They knew Babylonian-style astronomy and cared that the temple's Sabbaths and feasts fell on the right days. The oldest Aramaic copies (4Q208–4Q211) come from the library later kept at Qumran.

title: The Four Quarters of the World
sum: Enoch names the four quarters of the world and explains each name. The east is "the first"; the south is where "the Most High will come down"; the west is "the Waning," where lights go down; the north holds three regions: the lands where people live, dark seas and forests, and the garden of righteousness.

Then he describes a map of the world: seven high mountains, seven great rivers flowing into the Great Sea and the Erythraean Sea, and seven great islands. The explanations of the names only work in Hebrew or Aramaic, a sign of the book's original language.

views.E: The south as the place of God's coming is read alongside the Bible's God who comes "from Teman" (Habakkuk 3:3).
views.H: The geography is the Near East after Alexander: the Mediterranean, the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, rivers like the Nile and Euphrates. The wordplays point to an Aramaic original, and Aramaic fragments survive.
views.J: Explaining directions by Hebrew wordplay is typical of Jewish learning; north as the "hidden" place returns in later Jewish mystical texts.
views.W: A glimpse of ancient Jewish geography and of how early readers placed Eden and God's dwelling.

deep.b: East, qedem, is also "front" and "first." South, darom, was explained by the Aramaic, as Milik reads it, from dar, "dwell": the Great One dwells there (see the variant on 77:1, known only from Milik's report); an older Hebrew wordplay heard it as dar rom, "the High One dwells." North, tsafon, sounds like tsafun, "hidden." The Ge'ez translator kept the explanations even where the puns no longer worked in his language, which is good evidence that he was translating, not writing freely.

title: Names and Phases of the Moon
sum: The sun has two names and the moon four, probably Hebrew words worn down in copying. The two great lights are the same size, but the sun has seven parts of light more than the moon.

The chapter then counts the moon's light up to full on the fifteenth day and down again day by day to dark. Months have 30 or 29 days; six of each make a moon year of 354 days, and each half of it, 177 days, ends five days behind the sun. The first day is "the new moon," because the light rises on it.

views.E: The moon's waxing and waning shows God's measured order, and the church still reckons its moveable feasts by the moon.
views.H: The counting in fifteenths matches Babylonian lunar tables (Enuma Anu Enlil, Tablet 14). Milik identified Aramaic fragments of parts of 78–79 at Qumran. The verse about the moon looking "like a man" remains unexplained.
views.N: New moons appear among the holy days that Paul says believers should not judge each other over (Colossians 2:16).
views.J: The new moon remained central in rabbinic Judaism, fixed by witnesses who saw the crescent (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 2).
views.W: An ancient lunar table, valued for history; most readers note how closely it tracks real phases despite its scheme.

title: The Lesson Complete
sum: Enoch tells Methuselah that the lesson is finished: "The whole law of the stars of the sky is complete" (79:1). He sums up what Uriel showed him about days, seasons, years, months and weeks, and repeats the key numbers: the moon's waning in 177 days, "twenty-five weeks and two days," five days short of the sun's half year.
The chapter closes the first, purely astronomical part of the book. What follows (80–82) turns from numbers to warnings, blessings and Enoch's charge to his son.

views.E: Henok's teaching is complete and trustworthy because an angel gave it.
views.H: 79:1 and 79:6 look like the original ending of an astronomical treatise, to which chapters 80–82 were later joined. The Aramaic of 79:2–5 is reported among the Qumran fragments (Milik).
views.W: The weekly count ("weeks," literally "Sabbaths") shows how much the week mattered to this calendar, as it did to the Bible's Sabbath law.

settings.when: at the end of the astronomical lessons
settings.why: To mark the teaching as complete and exact, so that Methuselah can hand it on without adding or taking away.
settings.readers: A circle of learned Jewish scribes in Judea, probably with priestly ties, in the 200s BC or earlier. They knew Babylonian-style astronomy and cared that the temple's Sabbaths and feasts fell on the right days. The oldest Aramaic copies (4Q208–4Q211) come from the library later kept at Qumran.

title: When the Sky Loses Its Order
sum: Uriel ends his lessons with a warning. "In the days of the sinners" the years will be shortened, crops will be late, rain will stop, the moon will change its order and many leaders of the stars will stray from God's command. People will lose track of the true order and "treat the stars as gods."

After eight chapters of calm tables this is poetry about sin and judgment. The order of the sky now becomes a moral mirror: when people turn from God's ways, even the calendar seems to fall apart around them.
readings: Read as prophecy of the end
Like Mark 13 and Joel 2, the chapter foretells signs in the sun, moon and stars before the judgment.
The "shortened" years and late harvests may describe how a wrong calendar looks to those who keep the 364-day year: feasts drift out of their seasons, and the moon "changes its order."

views.E: A true prophecy of the last days, read beside the Gospels' signs in sun, moon and stars.
views.H: Probably added when the Astronomical Book was joined to the rest of 1 Enoch; no Aramaic of it has been identified. It ties astronomy to the judgment themes of the Watchers and the Epistle.
views.N: Compare the shortened days and cosmic signs of Mark 13:20–25 and Matthew 24:22–29, and the "wandering stars" of Jude 13.
views.J: Jubilees makes the same link: forgetting the true year leads Israel to keep feasts on the wrong days (Jubilees 6:34–38).
views.W: Christian readers find here the Bible's own warning against star worship (Deuteronomy 4:19), in strong agreement with Scripture.

deep.title: "The years will be shortened" as the moon's year
deep.b: My suggestion: for people who believed in the 364-day year, the moon's year of 354 days was literally a "shortened" year, and a calendar built on it would make sowing and harvest feasts arrive "late" or early against the seasons (80:2–3), while the moon seemed to "change its order" (80:4). If so, chapter 80 is not only a vision of the end but a description of what the authors thought rival calendars were doing to Israel's worship. This overlaps with scholars who read 80:2–8 as calendar polemic, though the precise reading of "shortened years" as the lunar year is my own.

echoes: Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 11:16–17; Joel 2:10; Mark 13:20–25; Matthew 24:22–29; Jude 13; Romans 1:25; 4 Ezra 5:4–5

settings.what: Uriel's warning about the days of the sinners
settings.when: at the end of the lessons on the lights
settings.why: To show that the order Enoch has learned can be broken by sin, and that those who follow the true order must expect a world falling out of joint around them. Inside the story it warns Enoch's descendants.
settings.readers: Jewish readers in Judea, perhaps in the 200s or 100s BC, for whom keeping the right calendar was part of faithfulness, and who saw rival calendars and star worship around them.
views: Some scholars think 80:2–8 always followed the astronomical lessons as their warning.
Many think it was added, with chapter 81, when the book was joined to the rest of 1 Enoch.

title: The Heavenly Tablets
sum: Uriel tells Enoch to read "the book of the heavenly tablets," and Enoch reads the deeds of every human being to the last generation. He blesses God for his patience and pronounces a blessing on the one who dies righteous, with nothing written against him.

Then three holy ones bring Enoch home. He is to have one more year to teach and write for his children, because "no flesh is righteous before the Lord." The righteous will rejoice together; the sinners will die together. Enoch returns to his people blessing God.

views.E: Henok's last year on earth, after which God took him (Genesis 5:24), and the source of the books his family preserved.
views.H: Many scholars, including Nickelsburg, see 81:1–82:4 as a bridge written to join the Astronomical Book to the other Enoch writings and to frame them as Enoch's testament.
views.N: Background for the heavenly books of Daniel 7:10 and Revelation 20:12, for "no flesh is righteous" (Romans 3:20), and for Hebrews 11:5 on Enoch's being taken.
views.J: The heavenly tablets become a central idea in Jubilees; rabbinic tradition speaks instead of books opened on the New Year.
views.W: Read as a moving picture of judgment and grace, close to the Bible's teaching that no one is righteous before God.

deep.b: Chapter 81 does not mention the calendar at all. Its themes, the heavenly tablets, the deeds of all people, the righteous and the sinners, belong to the Epistle of Enoch (see 93:2; 103:2). Enoch is brought "back" home by three holy ones, though the astronomical chapters never said he left. For these reasons many scholars think 81:1–82:4 was written to tie the Astronomical Book into a larger collection, and to present all of Enoch's books as his testament to Methuselah.

echoes: Genesis 5:24; Psalm 139:16; Psalm 143:2; Daniel 7:10; Isaiah 57:1–2; Romans 3:20; Hebrews 11:5; Revelation 14:13; Revelation 20:12

settings.what: The heavenly tablets and Enoch's blessing
settings.by: Uriel speaks; Enoch answers with praise and a blessing
settings.to: Enoch; the blessing is for all who die righteous
settings.when: at the end of Enoch's heavenly journeys
settings.why: To show that the God who orders the sky also records every life, and to bless those whom the record does not condemn.
settings.readers: Jewish readers who knew the other Enoch books and treasured them as one testament, perhaps in the 100s BC.

settings.what: The holy ones' charge to Enoch
settings.to: Enoch, at the door of his house
settings.when: as they bring him back to earth for one last year
settings.why: To send Enoch to teach and write for his children, and to encourage the righteous: they will rejoice together even if they die because of the wicked.
settings.readers: A community that saw itself as the righteous among sinners, and needed courage when the righteous suffered.

title: Keep the Books, Count the Days
sum: Enoch gives Methuselah his books and his wisdom to pass on to every generation: wisdom sweeter than fine food. Then he blesses the righteous who "do not sin as the sinners do in counting all their days" (82:4): those who keep the four added days and the 364-day year.

The rest of the chapter names the angelic officers who lead the stars: four leaders of the seasons, twelve of the months, and heads of thousands over the days. Two seasons are described, spring under Milkiel and summer under Helemmelek, with their heat, harvests and flocks. Then the Ethiopic text breaks off.

views.E: Henok's charge to Methuselah is the reason his book survived to be read by the church. The Ethiopian church keeps its own calendar of feasts and fasts, and reads the blessing as a call to keep God's appointed times faithfully.
views.H: The blessing on those who count right shows that the calendar was a mark of the true community. The leaders' names and seasons are probably the oldest material; the book's ending is lost.
views.N: Background for Colossians 2:16 and Galatians 4:10, and for the argument, made by Annie Jaubert, that Jesus ate the Last Supper by the 364-day calendar.
views.J: The Qumran texts and Jubilees put all the feasts on this year; the temple and the rabbis kept the moon year. The quarrel is visible in the Qumran account of the Wicked Priest's attack on the Day of Atonement.
views.W: Christian readers usually value the chapter for history, and set beside it Paul's teaching that believers must not judge one another over days (Romans 14:5–6).

deep.b:
Feasts in the 364-day year

The year starts on a Wednesday, the fourth day, when God made the lights (Genesis 1:14–19), and every quarter starts on a Wednesday too, since 91 days are 13 weeks. So every date falls on the same weekday every year (dates as in Jubilees and the Qumran texts):

DayDateWeekday, every year
New YearMonth 1, day 1Wednesday
PassoverMonth 1, day 14Tuesday
Feast of WeeksMonth 3, day 15Sunday
Day of AtonementMonth 7, day 10Friday
Booths beginsMonth 7, day 15Wednesday

None of the great feasts can fall on a Sabbath, so no feast ever clashes with the Sabbath rest.

The first three Gospels present the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12); John dates the crucifixion to the day before Passover (John 18:28; John 19:14). In 1957 Annie Jaubert proposed that Jesus ate the Passover by the 364-day calendar, on Tuesday evening, and was crucified on Friday, the official Passover eve. She pointed to an early Christian church order, the Didascalia, which puts the Supper on a Tuesday. In a Holy Thursday homily (5 April 2007) Pope Benedict XVI called the Qumran-calendar solution highly plausible. In Jesus of Nazareth (2011) he set Jaubert's theory aside and held instead, with John P. Meier, that Jesus ate a farewell meal before Passover, as John's dating implies. Most scholars doubt it, because nothing in the Gospels suggests Jesus followed a sectarian calendar.

It appears in 1 Enoch 72–82, in Jubilees, and in many Dead Sea Scrolls: calendar texts with the rota of priestly divisions (4Q319–4Q330), the Temple Scroll's feasts, and the list that opens 4Q394. Whether the Jerusalem temple ever used it is debated: some scholars (Jaubert, VanderKam) think it is an old priestly calendar that the temple gave up; others think it was always the ideal of a dissenting group. It never became the calendar of the Jewish people.
The Ethiopic text ends at 82:20 with only two of the four seasons described. Chapter 83 begins a different work, the Dream Visions.

echoes: Leviticus 23:4; Psalm 19:10; Isaiah 40:26; Isaiah 55:8–9; Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5–6; Galatians 4:10; Mark 14:12; John 18:28; Jubilees 6:32–38; Jubilees 7:38–39

settings.when: in Enoch's last year on earth (81:6)
settings.why: To hand on the books and to bless those who keep the true calendar. It tells later readers that the books are an inheritance from before the flood, and that faithfulness includes keeping God's appointed times.

settings.why: To show that every day of the year has its appointed officer, so that nothing in God's order is left uncounted.

traditions.q: Must God's people keep a set calendar of holy days?
views: Yes, the church's calendar of feasts and fasts binds the faithful: Wednesdays and Fridays, the great fasts and the feasts of the Lord, Mary, the angels and the saints. The church follows the Alexandrian 365-day year, not the 364-day year of 1 Enoch.

The Church sets the liturgical year, and the faithful must keep Sunday and the holy days of obligation (Catechism 1163–1171, 2177; Code of Canon Law 1246). Colossians 2:16 is read as freedom from the Jewish law's calendar, not from the Church's feasts.
The church year, with Pascha fixed by the rule of the Council of Nicaea (325), shapes all of life. The churches are divided over the old Julian calendar and the revised calendar of 1923.

Only the Lord's Day is commanded. The Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645) says festival days "having no warrant in the word of God, are not to be continued." Many Reformed churches today keep Christmas and Easter as a matter of freedom.
The seventh-day Sabbath, Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, is God's commandment for all people (Fundamental Beliefs, 20). The yearly feasts of Leviticus 23 are not binding.
